newsitem.title: FRANCE: Luxury goods giant LVMH profit falls on Guinness sale.
newsitem.headline: Luxury goods giant LVMH profit falls on Guinness sale.

text.p: Luxury goods giant LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton said Thursday its profits fell in 1996 after a loss on the sale of shares in British drinks group Guinness Plc.
LVMH sold a third of its Guinness stock to help pay for its $2.6 billion purchase of 61.25 percent of prestige retail chain Duty Free Shoppers.

Net attributable profit fell to 3.68 billion francs ($647.2 million) from 4.05 billion ($710.5 million) in 1995 after the company took a 615 million franc ($107.9 million) charge due mainly to the capital loss on the Guinness sale, LVMH said.

Profit excluding exceptional items rose 6 percent to 4.3 billion francs ($7.54 billion), helped by a 5 percent rise in sales, sharply reduced financial expenses and higher returns on its holding in Guinness, which was 14 percent at the end of the year.

LVMH's stock initally fell on the results but recovered after Chairman Bernard Arnault said the company would amortize the DFS stake over 40 years, and not over 25 to 30 as previously envisaged. A spokeswoman said this meant the goodwill amortisation would weigh less on annual results.
Arnault said LVMH suspended its efforts to buy out DFS minority shareholder Robert Miller after talks became difficult, but he did not rule out an eventual deal.
Miller said Wednesday that LVMH reneged on an agreement in principle to buy his stake and he expected to take legal action.

LVMH has also been challenged in court over its other recent acquisition, the Chateau d'Yquem vineyard which makes Sauterne wines. Manager and minority owner Count Alexandre de Lur-Saluces contests a deal by other family members to sell 55 percent.

LVMH, whose products span the range of French luxury goods from Moet Chandon champagnes to Louis Vuitton designer luggage and Christian Dior perfumes, reported a 4 percent drop in operating profit to 7.02 billion francs ($1.23 billion) from 7.29 billion ($1.28 billion).

It said the drop was partly due to lower sales and profits on perfumes and beauty products following LVMH's campaign to block sales to parallel channels that supply discounters, tarnishing the image of its Christian Dior and other perfumes.
Officials said they expected the sector to recover in 1997.

Sales and profits also fell at the cognac and spirits division, reflecting shrunken corporate entertainment budgets in Japan. The yen's fall against the franc further weighed on the division's results.
